t: ‘Thracians’ was the Greek name for some 200 tribes of south-eastern Europe who shared much of their culture but were rarely united in one state.
Greek and Roman writers called them warlike barbarians while hiring them as mercenaries and noting their poetry and music; the fairness of these accounts is now questioned.
Their tombs and gold and silver treasures, studied mainly in Bulgaria and Romania, give a fuller picture of a people gradually absorbed into Roman, Byzantine and Slavic societies.
dyk: In 570 CE Antoninus Placentius reported a monastery in the valleys of Mount Sinai whose monks spoke Greek, Latin, Syriac, Egyptian and Bessian, the language of a Thracian tribe.
ev: The first Greek colonies are founded on the Thracian coasts
The Thracian Treres, with the Cimmerians and Lycians, capture Sardis, the Lydian capital, except its citadel
Darius I of the Achaemenid Empire marches into Thrace and brings its tribes under Persian rule
Teres I founds the Odrysian Kingdom, the first lasting Thracian state
The Thracian gladiator Spartacus leads a great slave uprising in southern Italy
Thracia becomes a Roman province after the murder of King Rhoemetalces III
Antoninus Placentius records monks speaking Bessian at a monastery near Mount Sinai
Intensive excavations in Bulgaria uncover many Thracian tombs and sanctuaries

f.homeland: Bulgaria, Romania, North Macedonia, northern Greece and European Turkey, with north-western Anatolia; key sites Seuthopolis, Perperikon, Tatul, Starosel, the Valley of the Thracian Rulers with the Tomb of Kazanlak, the Tomb of Sveshtari
f.period: Thracian culture emerged in the early Bronze Age; first named in Homer’s Iliad; Greek colonies on its coasts from the 8th century BCE; Odrysian Kingdom from the early 5th century BCE; Roman province of Thracia from 46 CE; last reported use of a Thracian language in the 6th century CE
f.known: skilled horsemen and peltasts; the rhomphaia; gold and silver treasures such as Panagyurishte and Rogozen; the cult of the Thracian horseman; early worship of Dionysus; tattooing; poetry and music; mercenaries
f.sources: Greek and Roman writers (Homer, Herodotus, Thucydides, Xenophon, Strabo, Tacitus), Persian sources and reliefs, four short Thracian inscriptions, tombs, sanctuaries and treasures studied by Thracology, DNA studies
